files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller’s checklist

Owner: B. Okafor. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 and paying in July. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first to prevent duplication. If the entry is missing, book June prepaid amortization as ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after first verifying what is already recorded in the GL.
5. Inspect the June vendor-bill documents against the GL, verify that each expense is coded to the correct account, and reclass anything miscoded.
6. After items 1-5 are posted, prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Bluebird Wholesale Co. began in 2018 when two former purchasing managers saw an opening between large national distributors and the independent businesses those distributors often overlooked. They started with a compact assortment of shipping materials, breakroom goods, cleaning products, and everyday operating supplies, emphasizing practical pack sizes and dependable service rather than an enormous catalog.

The company now serves regional retailers, offices, food-service operators, and light industrial customers. Its buyers keep the assortment focused, while the warehouse crew is known for catching unusual order requests before they become picking problems. The sales team tends to know customers by name, and the operations staff maintains a running collection of handwritten notes about delivery preferences, loading access, and seasonal demand.

Bluebird Wholesale Co. remains an ordinary, active wholesale business. The current priority is balancing responsive service with tighter purchasing discipline and cleaner product data. Management is also refining vendor relationships, improving inventory visibility, and giving the sales team more consistent marketing support. The culture is informal but accountable: quick conversations are common, yet the team expects orders, records, and customer commitments to be handled carefully.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Position Bluebird Wholesale Co. as the practical regional supplier for customers who value responsive service, sensible assortments, and straightforward fulfillment.

## Priorities

- Refresh the brand voice and core sales materials without losing the company’s familiar, approachable tone.
- Run two educational webinars per quarter, centered on inventory planning, supply-room efficiency, and seasonal ordering.
- Pilot a partner co-marketing program with selected vendors and complementary service providers.
- Build reusable product spotlights for email, sales follow-up, and account reviews.
- Give the sales team short customer stories and category talking points that are easy to personalize.

## Quarterly emphasis

**Q3:** Complete the messaging refresh, prepare the webinar format, and recruit pilot partners. Test a regular email cadence with existing customers.

**Q4:** Expand the strongest webinar topics, publish partner content, and equip account managers with year-end planning materials.

## Measures

Track registrations, attendance quality, customer replies, sales-team usage, partner participation, and follow-up conversations. Review results after each campaign and keep only the formats that create useful customer engagement.

Budget remains pending completion of the Q2 close.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from the previous accountant

B. Okafor — a few things worth knowing before you finish the close:

- The bank usually places its own fees and charges near the end of the statement. We do not record those during the month; they get booked as part of close.
- Please look closely at June vendor-bill coding. A couple of expenses may be sitting in the wrong accounts, and the documents in `bills/` are the authoritative source when the GL and the paperwork disagree.
- The Q2 budget was locked in early April. The one-off items that arrived in June were never included, so they are the main reason some variances look unusually large.
- Payroll timing is different this time: the second June run pays in early July. Confirm it against the payroll register.
